chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Al-Fudayl from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

If a free person confesses to theft once before the Imam, the hand is cut off. The approach in this narration is to interpret it as being based on taqiyyah (dissimulation), because it agrees with the view of some of the Sunnis. As for the narrations we cited in the book *Tahdib al-Ahkam* stating that when the thief confesses, the hand is cut off, they are general (mujmal) and do not specify whether he confessed in one instance or two. It is appropriate to interpret them according to the specification contained in the first report, which adds clarity to this.

key_terms.الْحُرُّ: The free person (as opposed to a slave)

ai.seo_question: How does Shia jurisprudence reconcile the requirement of one versus two confessions for cutting the hand in theft?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent contradiction between a narration requiring only one confession for hand amputation and others implying multiple confessions by attributing the single-confession ruling to *taqiyyah*, thereby aligning it with Sunni jurisprudence. He clarifies that the general narrations are *mujmal* (unspecified) and must be interpreted through the specific detail of the first report, establishing a nuanced Shia legal methodology for reconciling conflicting texts. This approach highlights the Shia emphasis on contextualizing narrations rather than accepting them at face value when discrepancies arise with established Sunni positions.
